design_detail: Umbrella review plus top-up systematic review, commissioned by the Australian Department of Health, of the health effects of e-cigarettes in humans (nicotine and non-nicotine; tetrahydrocannabinol products, animal, in-vitro and biomarker studies excluded when possible). The umbrella part starts from the 2018 National Academies report and eight major independent reviews (2017 to 2021); the top-up part searched six databases in July 2020 for studies from July 2017 to July 2020 not in the National Academies report. 400 publications were synthesised narratively by health outcome, with conclusions worded on the National Academies evidence scale and the certainty of each outcome rated with GRADE. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42020200673 (top-up systematic review). Pooled estimates quoted come from the authors' earlier reviews, not new meta-analyses.
can_establish: What a government-commissioned, two-reviewer synthesis of studies up to mid-2020 (and of major reviews up to 2021) concluded about each type of health outcome of e-cigarette use, how strong it rated the evidence, and which outcomes had no usable studies.
cannot_establish: Anything after mid-2020 (the two PATH cohort papers on heart and lung disease read for this batch came later), pooled effect sizes (the main text reports no pooled estimate of its own; the Methods say meta-analyses were done when possible and refer to the supplement), the relative harm of vaping against smoking (the authors state that comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health impact of e-cigarettes, and the review excludes biomarker studies), or the content of the 400 studies (the evidence tables are in a supplement that was not read).

sample.recruitment: Top-up search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, the Cochrane Library and PsycINFO in July 2020 for peer-reviewed human studies published July 2017 to July 2020, plus forward and backward citation searching, one grey-literature item, and 37 studies from the authors' two earlier reviews of smoking uptake and cessation; umbrella part: grey-literature search for major reviews to 31 December 2021 (later reviews to November 2022 considered in the discussion only) (Methods; Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Peer-reviewed original research on health effects of e-cigarettes. Excluded when possible: e-cigarettes delivering THC, animal, in vitro and biomarker studies. 86 publications excluded because the design precluded causal inference; three otherwise eligible studies excluded for low quality scores. Cessation analyses limited to randomized trials with biochemically verified cessation and at least four months' follow-up. Design order of preference: randomized trials, prospective cohorts, case-control, non-randomized intervention studies; other designs when these were unavailable.
sample.demographics: Not summarised in the text; evidence tables are in the supplement (parts 3 and 4, not read). Nicotine content was generally not reported, and the authors assumed reported effects concerned nicotine-containing products unless stated.
sample.selection_effects: The review answers the questions its design can: acute and device-related outcomes, dependence, smoking uptake and cessation. Excluding biomarker and cross-sectional-only evidence for causal questions removes the exposure data that other reviews rely on (for example the PATH biomarker comparison). The search ends in July 2020, so the longitudinal cohort papers on heart and lung disease published later are not in it. 126 of the 400 publications (about 31%, editors' count from Box 2) are surveillance reports, case series and case reports on burns, injuries and poisoning, which can show that a harm occurs but not how often.

exposure.measurement: E-cigarette use as defined by each included study; most did not report e-cigarette type or e-liquid contents, and the authors note products labelled nicotine-free often contain nicotine.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesised; the review notes long-term evidence is unavailable and that the products studied do not necessarily reflect current devices (for example nicotine-salt pods).
exposure.polysubstance: Outcomes are reported separately for people who smoke and people who do not; dual use is described as the most common pattern in many countries, with unknown direct health impact (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

comparison.controls: Varies by study. The authors state that people neither smoking nor using e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, and that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, because statistical adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding by smoking (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level; the authors name residual confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking as a major problem.

outcomes.instruments: Outcomes grouped by organ system or event (clinical disease endpoints, subclinical outcomes, other); conclusions worded on the National Academies scale (conclusive, substantial, moderate, limited, insufficient, no available evidence) and the certainty of each integrated body of evidence rated with GRADE (supplement part 2, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: Methodological quality of top-up studies assessed independently by two authors with Joanna Briggs Institute checklists; the included major reviews are not formally appraised, though the authors rate the 2022 Cochrane review as less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No available evidence' means no included studies on the outcome; 'insufficient' means studies exist but cannot support a conclusion.

analysis.effect_sizes: No new pooled estimates are reported in the main text. Counts per outcome (Box 2/3): dependence 52, cardiovascular disease 21 (1 meta-analysis, 11 randomized trials, 1 cohort, 7 non-randomized intervention studies, 1 case report), cancer 1, respiratory disease 58 (10 randomized trials, 6 cohorts, 8 non-randomized intervention studies, 18 surveillance reports, 7 case series, 9 case reports), burns and injuries 67, poisoning 59, less serious adverse events 47, smoking uptake 28, cessation 11; smaller categories: oral health 4, developmental and reproductive 3, mental health 3, environmental hazards 25, neurological 13, ocular 1, olfactory 1, endocrine 2, allergy 4, sleep, wound healing and haematological 0. Editors' check: the row totals in Box 2 add to 400, and the selection arithmetic works (227 + 10 + 1 - 86 + 37 = 189 top-up studies; 112 + 189 + 99 = 400).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42020200673, posted 31 August 2020 according to the Methods, which is after the July 2020 search; the abstract calls the registration prospective. Only the top-up systematic review is registered; deviations are not discussed; search strategy and GRADE method are in the supplement (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The main text reports conclusions by outcome rather than study-level data; which individual studies drove each conclusion cannot be checked without the supplement.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As of studies to mid-2020 (and major reviews to 2021), the review rated the evidence as conclusive for poisoning, burns and injuries, seizures and e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (largely THC products), substantial for dependence in people who do not smoke, moderate for acute rises in heart rate, blood pressure and arterial stiffness in people who smoke and for mild adverse events, limited (people who do not smoke) or insufficient (people who smoke) for acute changes in spirometry, insufficient (people who smoke) or no available evidence (people who do not smoke) for asthma, bronchitis and COPD, and 'no available evidence' for heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death and cancer. It rated certainty for clinical and subclinical outcomes low or very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that e-cigarettes 'can be harmful to health', particularly for non-smokers, children, adolescents and young adults, that effects on many important outcomes are uncertain, and that they may benefit smokers who use them to quit completely and promptly. The Discussion goes further in places: it says there is evidence of adverse effects on lung function (Box 3 rates this limited or insufficient), cites human and animal studies on nicotine and adolescent brain development (the review excluded animal studies and rates development outcomes 'no available evidence'), applies the precautionary principle, and says the evidence supports policy to reduce use in the general population. The Results describe the cessation trials as showing e-cigarettes 'as efficacious as' nicotine replacement while Box 4 says 'more efficacious than'.

timeline.event: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine report: the starting point of this umbrella review; 112 of its 400 publications come from it, so the two are not independent (card sc_nasem_2018).

McNeill et al., Nicotine vaping in England: identified by the authors after their umbrella search and described as lacking direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and as finding more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes, mainly on comparisons with smoking and biomarkers (card sc_mcneill_2022).

Mendelsohn et al. published a critique whose title names the report on which this article is based (reference 13 here, 'Electronic cigarettes and health outcomes: systematic review of global evidence'); it was not read for this card, so what it criticises is not recorded here.

Cochrane review of e-cigarettes for smoking cessation (Hartmann-Boyce et al., 2022 update): discussed by the authors, who rate it less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials and note it rated trial risk of bias lower than they did; not read here.

replication.where_it_stands: A government-commissioned synthesis whose conclusions on chronic disease ('no available evidence', 'insufficient') describe the state of the literature in 2020 to 2021, before the PATH cohort papers on heart and lung disease. It agrees broadly with the major reviews it builds on, which share much of its evidence. A published critique is listed in the library and has not been read.

funding.funder: Australian Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC), as part of an independent program examining the health impacts of e-cigarettes; Banks holds an NHMRC Principal Research Fellowship (1136128). The work was commissioned by the Department of Health and its report also informed the 2021 RACGP smoking-cessation guideline update and a 2022 NHMRC statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: 'No relevant disclosures.' The report on which the article is based was reviewed by members of the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and staff of the Department of Health, and subject to an independent methodological review under NHMRC processes.
funding.affiliations_note: All authors are at the National Centre for Epidemiology and Population Health, Australian National University. No tobacco, e-cigarette or pharmaceutical funding is declared. The commissioning body is a government health department; its staff and an NHMRC committee reviewed the underlying report, which the article says also went through an independent methodological review.

what_would_settle_it: An update of the same review with a search beyond 2020 that includes the longitudinal cohort studies of heart and lung disease and any trials with clinical endpoints, appraised with a risk-of-bias tool for non-randomized studies of exposures, with published evidence tables and a list of excluded studies, and with a pre-specified decision on how to treat comparisons with smoking.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans), exposure (e-cigarette use, with and without nicotine) and outcomes (health outcomes grouped by system) are stated, with an order of preferred designs; no comparator is part of the eligibility criteria. Comparison groups (people who do or do not smoke; people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes) are set outcome by outcome in the synthesis.
PROSPERO record for the top-up review, dated 31 August 2020, after the July 2020 search; the paper calls it prospective; deviations and a synthesis plan are not described in the main text.

A stated order of preference (randomized trials, prospective cohorts, case-control, non-randomized intervention) and the reason (suitability for causal inference), with other designs used where these were unavailable.

Six databases, citation searching and a grey-literature search for major reviews; terms are in the supplement (not read); no registry search is described; the main search ended in July 2020, about two and a half years before publication.
Two authors screened all titles, abstracts and articles independently; disagreements by consensus or a third author.
One author extracted with a piloted template and a second checked the data (not fully independent duplicate extraction).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: The text gives reasons in aggregate (86 excluded for design, three for low quality, three cited) and a selection figure (Box 1, an image); a list of excluded studies may be in the supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Counts by outcome and design in Box 2; study-level descriptions are in the supplement (parts 3 and 4, not read).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Joanna Briggs Institute checklists by two authors independently, with low-quality studies excluded; individual ratings and the handling of confounding are not shown in the main text.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and competing interests of each study were noted at extraction and used in the risk-of-bias assessment; whether they are reported per study is in the supplement (not read).

The Methods say meta-analyses were conducted when possible (supplement, part 2), but the main text presents no pooled estimate of its own; the pooled figures it quotes (smoking uptake) come from the authors' earlier review (reference 18) and published meta-analyses. Whether this item applies can be judged only from the supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: As item 11: depends on whether pooled analyses exist in the supplement.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Risk of bias and competing interests fed the GRADE ratings, certainty is stated as low or very low for most clinical and subclinical outcomes, and the Discussion says risk-of-bias concerns were outweighed by other domains.
Inconsistency is named as a reason for low certainty, but no heterogeneity is quantified or explained in the main text; the GRADE reasons are in the supplement (part 5, not read).
Publication bias is not discussed in the main text; whether a quantitative synthesis exists in the supplement (see item 11) is not known.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funders and the absence of competing interests are stated; the commissioner's staff and a committee reviewed the underlying report.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 7, 10, 11, 12 and 15 can be judged only from the supplement or the full report, which were not read. If one of the critical items 7, 11 or 15 proved to be 'no', AMSTAR 2 would give low confidence; if two did, critically low. On the items that can be judged from the main text, no critical item is 'no' (2, 4 and 9 are partly met), and the confirmed weaknesses are non-critical (1: no comparator in the eligibility criteria; 14: heterogeneity not explained in the main text); data extraction was by one author with a second author checking (item 6, scored 'yes' as in sc_hartmann_boyce_2023, though AMSTAR 2 strictly asks for two extractors or good agreement on a sample). More than one non-critical weakness and no confirmed critical flaw gives moderate confidence at best. This is a judgment about the review's method, not about its policy conclusions. It may be cited for what the literature to 2020 and 2021 contained on each outcome and for the National Academies-scale wording of its conclusions (for example 'no available evidence' for clinical heart disease and cancer, 'insufficient' for asthma, bronchitis and COPD); not for the size of any risk, for evidence after mid-2020, for relative harm against smoking (which it does not assess: its authors say comparisons with smoking cannot reliably show the direct health impact, and it excludes biomarker studies), or as independent confirmation of the National Academies report, from which 112 of its 400 studies come.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC10952413 (all main-text sections, Boxes 2 to 4 as text, acknowledgements, competing interests, reference list; Box 1 is an image and was not extracted; Supporting Information (search terms, GRADE method, evidence tables, certainty reasons) not read; the full report to the Department of Health not read)

key_findings.finding: Method: umbrella review starting from the 2018 National Academies report and a grey-literature search for major independent reviews to 31 December 2021 (eight included), plus a top-up systematic review of six databases searched in July 2020 for studies from July 2017 to July 2020, with two authors screening independently and Joanna Briggs Institute appraisal by two authors; PROSPERO CRD42020200673.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Umbrella review; Methods › Top-up review; Methods › Eligibility screening and Risk of bias assessment; Abstract › Registration

key_findings.finding: Selection: 6558 potentially eligible records; 227 eligible, plus ten from citation searching and one from grey literature; 86 excluded because the design precluded causal inference; 37 added from two earlier reviews by the authors, giving 189 top-up studies; with 112 from the National Academies report and 99 from other reviews, 400 publications in the synthesis. THC products, animal, in vitro and biomarker studies were excluded when possible.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Inclusion and exclusion criteria

key_findings.finding: Counts of studies by outcome (Box 2): cardiovascular disease 21 (1 meta-analysis, 11 randomized trials, 1 cohort, 7 non-randomized intervention studies, 1 case report); cancer 1 (a cohort); respiratory disease 58 (10 randomized trials, 6 cohorts, 8 non-randomized intervention studies, 18 surveillance reports, 7 case series, 9 case reports).

Cardiovascular conclusions (Box 3): clinical outcomes (heart attack, stroke, cardiovascular death) and subclinical atherosclerosis outcomes: no available evidence; blood pressure, heart rate, arterial stiffness and related measures in non-smokers: insufficient evidence; in smokers: moderate evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes acutely raise heart rate, systolic and diastolic blood pressure and arterial stiffness, limited evidence of raised endothelial dysfunction and limited evidence that long-term use after switching from smoking lowers blood pressure.

Respiratory conclusions (Box 3): lung injury (EVALI) conclusive, largely with THC products, but in the largest study 14% of cases were in people reporting only nicotine products and 2% non-nicotine products; asthma, bronchitis and COPD: insufficient evidence in smokers, no available evidence in non-smokers; fewer exacerbations or less progression after switching: insufficient; acute spirometry changes: limited (non-smokers) or insufficient (smokers); airway resistance after use: limited.
key_findings.locator: Box 3, row 'Respiratory disease (58)'; Results › Health outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Cancer (Box 3): invasive cancer risk and pre-cancer outcomes: no available evidence (one included study).

Certainty: rated low or very low for clinical and subclinical outcomes, because of small samples, study design and a paucity of evidence that caused serious concerns about inconsistency, imprecision and indirectness. The authors conclude the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health outcomes, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Other conclusions: conclusive evidence for poisoning, nicotine toxicity, burns and injuries, seizures and (largely THC-related) lung injury; substantial evidence that nicotine e-cigarettes cause dependence in non-smokers and limited evidence in smokers (including limited evidence that abuse liability is lower than for cigarettes); moderate evidence for throat irritation, cough, dizziness, headache and nausea.
key_findings.locator: Results › Health outcomes, 1st paragraph; Box 3, rows 'Dependence and abuse liability (52)', 'Poisoning', 'Less serious adverse events (47)'

key_findings.finding: On relative harm: the authors state that people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, that people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, that adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking, that statements such as 'safer than smoking' may be useful for the minority of smokers who quit completely but do not apply to non-smokers, and that comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

The authors describe an English review (McNeill et al., 2022, found after their search) as noting the lack of direct evidence on major clinical outcomes and that most serious adverse events were infrequent, and as focusing on comparisons with smoking and biomarkers, where it generally found more favourable results for e-cigarettes than for cigarettes. They rate the 2022 Cochrane cessation review as less independent because four of its authors were investigators in included trials.

Dual use is the most frequent pattern of e-cigarette use in many countries; its direct health impact is unknown, and e-cigarettes may facilitate continued smoking. Smokers who quit completely and promptly by switching may benefit. E-cigarettes are not registered therapeutic goods in Australia.

Authors' stated limits: products are new, diverse and changing; long-term evidence is unavailable; most publications lack e-cigarette type and e-liquid constituents, and products labelled nicotine-free often contain nicotine; confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking is a major problem. Risk of bias also considered competing interests such as tobacco or pharmaceutical funding.

Funding: Australian Department of Health and NHMRC; competing interests 'No relevant disclosures'; the report was reviewed by the NHMRC Electronic Cigarettes Working Committee and Department staff and by an independent methodological review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe the eleven cessation trials as showing freebase nicotine e-cigarettes with clinical support 'as efficacious' as nicotine replacement or usual care, while Box 4 says 'more efficacious' than nicotine replacement or no intervention (both labelled limited evidence).
reporting_issues.locator: Results › Smoking behaviour, 2nd paragraph; Box 4, row 'Smoking and nicotine cessation (11)'
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of the cessation conclusion is worded two ways in the same paper; claims on cessation should rely on the Cochrane card instead.

reporting_issues.issue: Box 3 rates 'Development of children or adolescents' as 'no available evidence', and acute spirometry effects as limited (non-smokers) or insufficient (smokers), but the Discussion says there is evidence for adverse effects on lung function and cites human and animal studies for adverse effects of nicotine on adolescent brain development.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite Box 3 for the rated conclusions; the Discussion sentences rely on sources outside the review's inclusion criteria.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods date the PROSPERO posting 31 August 2020, after the July 2020 search, while the abstract labels the registration prospective.
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether registration preceded screening and extraction cannot be checked from the text; item 2 is rated partial.

reporting_issues.issue: Pooled figures for smoking uptake (about three times the likelihood of starting to smoke) and the claim that the relationship was deemed likely causal come from the authors' own earlier meta-analysis (reference 18), summarised without new data.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not independent evidence; cite the earlier paper if the figure is needed.
